body.text: As Washington tightens access to advanced computing, Beijing is using APEC to promote AI cooperation and deepen regional economic integration, writes Vikas Kumar.
New restrictions on transfers and exports of AI semiconductors

On the eve of this week’s APEC Economic Leader’s Meeting in Shenzhen, the United States announced new restrictions on transfers and exports of advanced AI semiconductors, extending licensing requirements to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. The measures also target access by Chinese companies to significant computing capacity at overseas data centres.

The announcement follows the controversy surrounding the resignation of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang and investigations into Singapore-based computing provider Megaspeed over suspected diversion of advanced chips to China. Megaspeed maintains that it complies with export controls. Whatever the investigations ultimately establish, Washington’s move demonstrates how restrictions initially aimed at China can have wider consequences for regional economies.

The timing is striking. China is using its APEC host year to promote regional AI cooperation just as the US given the timing, is tightening the conditions under which advanced computing technology can be accessed. For decades, the Asia-Pacific has become interconnected through trade, investment and manufacturing networks. AI is adding a new dimension to that interdependence, even as competition between the great powers threatens to fragment it.
AI as a new form of connectivity

Last week, I was in Chengdu presenting research on the AI stack and the changing geography of international business at the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China. Chengdu also hosted APEC’s Digital and AI Ministerial Meeting in July. Building on the regional AI initiative endorsed in South Korea in 2025, the Chengdu Statement encourages cooperation on digital infrastructure, industrial AI adoption, workforce skills and trustworthy open-source technologies.

In Shenzhen, China is seeking agreement on a proposed leaders’ statement on AI and the digital economy, alongside initiatives on digital trade and connectivity. There is an important economic logic to these proposals. A manufacturer sourcing components across Asian economies could use AI to improve demand forecasting and inventory management, while interoperable customs systems and electronic trade documentation could reduce border delays. The benefits increase when suppliers can exchange information efficiently and smaller firms can afford to participate.

Yet AI integration requires access to computing infrastructure. In October, APEC finance ministers endorsed a policy statement on financing digital infrastructure. A Malaysian data centre operator reliant on American chips and Chinese customers may now face licensing requirements on both sides of its business model. This complicates investment decisions in the very infrastructure APEC is seeking to expand.
Competition through cooperation

China’s international AI ambitions extend well beyond APEC. In July, President Xi Jinping announced 5,000 AI training and seminar opportunities for developing countries over five years and plans for AI application cooperation centres with regional groupings including ASEAN.

Chinese companies are building commercial infrastructure alongside these diplomatic initiatives. In April, Huawei Cloud expanded its model-as-a-service offering to nine additional countries, including Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, offering access to models developed by DeepSeek, Alibaba and Zhipu. Alibaba Cloud also operates computing infrastructure across Southeast Asia.

Open-weight models allow local developers to adapt technology to local languages and industries. Their diffusion can generate demand for complementary products such as cloud services, hardware and enterprise applications, even when developers do not charge for access to model weights. China can therefore gain technological influence without necessarily leading at the model frontier.

The US has its own strategy. Its July 2025 executive order on exporting American AI technology established a programme to promote integrated packages of chips, computing services, models and applications internationally. Both countries seek to embed their technologies in other economies.

The new US rules, however, create an asymmetry. Under specified reporting conditions, US-headquartered companies and subsidiaries with US-headquartered ultimate parents are exempt from the new destination-based licensing requirements. Local data centre operators could face greater regulatory uncertainty and higher compliance costs than their American competitors, although restrictions on sensitive end uses still apply.

There is a potential unintended consequence for Washington. As access to American infrastructure becomes more conditional, businesses and governments may have stronger incentives to explore Chinese alternatives. Nvidia’s hardware and software advantages remain formidable, but the new restrictions could strengthen the commercial appeal of China’s efforts to provide alternative computing and AI services.
The opportunity for regional economies

For many Asian economies, the immediate opportunity lies in applying AI to raise productivity. The Pacific Economic Cooperation Council’s latest State of the Region report, released before the summit, highlights the challenge. Some 79 per cent of survey respondents identified digital skills as important to AI adoption, yet just 6 per cent regarded their economy as very prepared for workforce reskilling.

Access to affordable technology is valuable, but dependence on a particular ecosystem can deepen as firms train employees, adapt applications and organise their data around it. Governments should therefore judge AI partnerships by the domestic capabilities they create and the ability they allow for local firms to change suppliers when better technologies emerge.
What Australia should seek from Shenzhen

Australia should support practical APEC initiatives that improve interoperability between AI systems and strengthen domestic and regional capabilities. Our research and industry expertise could contribute to AI assurance, including joint testing facilities and cooperation on recognising safety and reliability assessments across markets. APEC’s voluntary, consensus-based approach offers scope for such cooperation even when members disagree on national security policy.

The juxtaposition of Washington’s new restrictions and Beijing’s cooperation agenda is a reminder that regional integration in the AI era cannot be taken for granted. The test of Shenzhen will be whether cooperation expands the technological choices available to Asia-Pacific economies, rather than leaving them dependent on one or another great power.
